outcomes.original: Filing step: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain a federal EIN from the IRS. What to say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at the CA Secretary of State bizfile portal. Within 90 days file the Statement of Information ($20 LLC, $25 corporation). Once the entity is registered, apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) online at IRS.gov (free, issued same day Mon–Fri). The EIN and entity name are required for the business registration, bank account, seller's permit, and all city permits.

Within 90 days file the Statement of Information ($20 LLC, $25 corporation). Once the entity is registered, apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) online at IRS.gov (free, issued same day Mon–Fri). The EIN and entity name are required for the business registration, bank account, seller's permit, and all city permits.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with SF Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN) and register for the California seller's permit with CDTFA. What to say: File online at sftreasurer.org for the SF Business Registration Certificate ($55–$700 tiered by gross receipts, plus $4 state fee). The BAN is required by every other city department. In parallel, register online at the CA Department of Tax and Fee Administration for the seller's permit (free; required to sell food and drink). Both take 1–5 days. If the public-facing restaurant name differs from the legal entity name, file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the SF County Clerk and publish it in a court-approved newspaper within 45 days.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit DPH health plan check application and building permit application with change-of-use routing to Planning in parallel. What to say: For DPH: apply online at sfdph.org/ehsportal with your BAN, Location ID (LIN) and EIN. Submit two sets of scaled floor plans, equipment layout, menu, finishes schedule, and hood/ventilation drawings. State that the project is a retail-to-restaurant change of use with full commercial cooking. DPH will route the application internally and assign a plan reviewer; fee is $828–$2,207 depending on scope (paid at application). For DBI: file a building permit application with tenant-improvement plans stamped by a licensed architect, showing the change of use from retail to restaurant. DBI will route the application to Planning under Planning Code § 175(a) for zoning conformity review and to DPH for concurrent review. State on the permit that the existing use is retail and the proposed use is restaurant, and that the project is subject to the health plan check already filed. Include mechanical,…

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (one manager) and enroll all employees in California Food Handler Card training. What to say: At least one owner or manager must pass an ANSI-accredited food safety exam (ServSafe, Prometric, NRFSP, 360training) within 60 days of opening; the certificate is valid 5 years and DPH asks for it at the pre-opening inspection ($100–$250, 1–14 days). Every employee who handles food must obtain a California Food Handler Card within 30 days of hire (online course, $7–$15, valid 3 years). Keep certificates on site for health inspections.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Respond to DPH and DBI plan-check corrections and coordinate Fire Department hood and ventilation sign-off; schedule pre-final and final inspections at ~80% and 100% construction complete. What to say: Work with your architect and mechanical engineer to address DPH and DBI comments on finishes, equipment, plumbing fixture counts, hood suppression system, grease interceptor, and ADA compliance. The Fire Department reviews the hood suppression system as part of the building permit; if the occupant load is 50 or more, a Place of Assembly permit is required from SFFD ($446). Schedule a DPH pre-final inspection at ~80% complete and a final pre-opening inspection when all equipment is installed, surfaces sealed, hand sinks operational, and hot water available; the health permit is issued after the final inspection passes. Schedule DBI final inspection to obtain the Certificate of Final Completion; Planning's zoning sign-off must be complete before DBI will finalize.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register with CA EDD for payroll taxes, obtain workers' compensation insurance, and subscribe to organics recycling service (SB 1383) before the first employee is hired or food waste is generated. What to say: Register as an employer at EDD's e-Services for Business within 15 days of paying more than $100 in wages (free, online, 1–7 days). Obtain workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund before hiring the first employee (mandatory from day one; quote through a broker). Contact your waste hauler (Recology in SF) to add organics (green bin) collection for commercial food generators per SB 1383; no permit required but the service must be in place before the health inspection.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File for exterior sign permit with Planning and DBI, and obtain ASCAP and BMI public performance licenses for recorded music. What to say: For signage: submit sign drawings to Planning for design review (size, illumination, historic-district compliance) and to DBI for permit issuance; fee is $300–$1,500, 7–45 days. For music: register online at ASCAP.com and BMI.com for blanket public performance licenses (formula-based fee, ~$300–$2,500/year each, effective immediately). Federal copyright law requires both licenses to play recorded music in a commercial space; the two catalogs do not overlap. Alternatively subscribe to a licensed commercial music service (e.g., Soundtrack Your Brand) that includes performance rights.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 49 to 255 days. Estimated government cost: $2,653 to $19,850. Notes: The timeline and cost cover the two approvals in the entitlement path (health permit to operate and building permit with change of use) plus their prerequisites, from entity formation through final inspection. The day range is the time to obtain those approvals when they are granted: health permit 14–45 days after plan check (21–60 days), building permit 14–120 days including Planning's zoning referral (14–90 days). If the zoning review determines that a Conditional Use Authorization is required (because the concept is formula retail, ≥2,501 sq ft, or closes after 11 p.m.), add 120–300 days and $3,100–$15,000 for the CUA hearing, which is not included here because the pathway status is insufficient information. The cost range includes: CA SOS LLC/corp ($70–$150), SF business registration ($55–$700), DPH health plan check ($828–$2,500), health permit application ($470–$1,000), building permit ($800–$15,000), Fire place-of-assembly permit if occupant load ≥50 ($446–$1,500), and sign permit ($300–$1,500). Not included: construction costs, architect and engineer fees, workers' comp insurance premiums (percentage of payroll), music licenses (~$600–$5,000/year), or a CUA filing fee. The timeline assumes plans are complete and responsive to plan-check corrections; incomplete submittals or failed inspections extend the schedule by weeks to months. The one health-referral denial in the candidate set (801 Kearny, 38 months to denial) shows that building readiness is the critical path risk.
